# Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) — concept pack (small)

> Source-anchored research for Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress). Run status: COMPLETED.

## Definitions

- [statement] Atlas Live Migration is a free MongoDB-hosted service, and MongoDB charges nothing for data transferred into an Atlas cluster. The tool and the inbound traffic add no Atlas line item. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/patterns/migrate-a-self-hosted-mongodb-environment-to-mongodb-atlas-on-the-aws-cloud.html

## Structure and components

- [statement] Exit waivers do not fund a partial move or a dual-run. Google's program bars migrating only part of a service; AWS scopes its waiver to all data off AWS or off one AWS service; Azure scopes its waiver to customers leaving Azure. A team that keeps part of its estate on the old cloud should assume list egress rates apply to the data it moves. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/free-data-transfer-out-to-internet-when-moving-out-of-aws/, https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/bandwidth/
- [statement] Google's exit process runs in stages: an Exit Notice, then 14 days for agent assignment and review, then a 30-day Initiation Period to start the move, then a Migration Period of at least 30 days (longer if Google or the customer asks for more time). A Completion Notice follows within 180 days, and termination takes effect at the next month end at least 30 days later. The program is per service, and moving only part of a given service is not permitted. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-09-11) — https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud
- [statement] A migration bill has these parts. This list is derived from the sources; it is not a published formula. Destination hours at the elevated tier through initial sync, lag drain, cutover and any hold. Source environment hours until the rollback window closes. Any staging cluster from a rehearsal. The mongosync host for standalone runs. Egress billed by the source provider. Application downtime. Exit-program credits offset only the egress part. The CMA's customer research found switches usually run two sets of services at once and keep the old one for a while in case of problems. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/<object-id>/Appendix_N_-_Egress_fees___free_switching_programmes.pdf, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration

## How it works

- [statement] Moving data into Atlas incurs no ingress fee: Atlas does not charge for incoming data transfer to an Atlas cluster, and AWS states there is no charge for inbound data transfer across all services in all Regions. The metered leg is the sender's egress, billed by the source's provider, or by Atlas when the source is an Atlas cluster. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/architecture/overview-of-data-transfer-costs-for-common-architectures/
- [statement] Atlas starts an extendable 120-hour (5-day) timer when it detects that source and destination are nearly in sync. When the timer expires, Atlas stops synchronizing and the user must retry the migration. The timer starts after the initial copy, so dual-running lasts the initial-copy time plus up to 120 hours, or more if the user extends the sync. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/
- [statement] In a mongosync cutover, application downtime runs from stopping writes on the source until the application can write to the destination after /progress reports canWrite: true. Start only when canCommit is true and lag.overallLagSeconds is near 0. If the embedded verifier is on, also require both verification documents to show lagTimeSeconds near 0 in the 'stream hashing' phase. If lag is not near 0 when cutover starts, the cutover can take a long time. With default settings mongosync blocks source writes once the user requests commit, and the user must first wait for open source transactions to commit or abort. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/cutover-process/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/about-mongosync/
- [statement] Google Cloud's free exit transfer (announced 11 January 2024) covers internet transfers off a Google Cloud service when the customer leaves that service completely, and only for products listed in Google's data-portability terms. Steps: submit an Exit Notice; Google assigns a billing-support agent within 14 days; the customer starts migrating within a 30-day Initiation Period; the Migration Period lasts at least 30 days; the customer sends a Completion Notice within 180 days after the Migration Period; the credit appears on the final invoice; the agreement for that service ends after at least 30 more days. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/networking/eliminating-data-transfer-fees-when-migrating-off-google-cloud
- [statement] The EU Data Act (Regulation (EU) 2023/2854) defines 'switching charges' to include data egress charges (Art. 2(35)-(36)); standard service fees and early termination penalties are outside the definition. From 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services may not impose any switching charges. From 11 January 2024 until 12 January 2027 they may impose only reduced charges that do not exceed their costs directly linked to the switching process (Art. 29(1)-(3)). (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2854 · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2025/07/understanding-switching-termination-rights-under-the-data-act
- [statement] A pull live migration is a bounded dual-running window. The source keeps taking writes while the destination, which is write-blocked, syncs. When the clusters are nearly in sync, Atlas starts an extendable cutover timer. When the timer expires, Atlas stops syncing from the source. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/live-migration-what-happens-if-if-you-miss-the-cut-over-window/101881
- [statement] AWS pays for leaving as credits, not as zero-rated traffic. AWS offers free data transfer out to the internet when a customer moves all data off AWS from all eligible payer accounts, or all data off one AWS service. The customer goes through AWS Support, and AWS applies extra scrutiny when the same account asks more than once. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-08) — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/free-data-transfer-out-to-internet-when-moving-out-of-aws/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/<object-id>/Appendix_N_-_Egress_fees___free_switching_programmes.pdf
- [statement] Google credits the egress on the customer's final invoice. The credit covers the workloads and production data on Google Cloud when the customer submitted the Exit Notice. The customer must submit the Exit Notice before any migration it expects a credit for. Free transfer covers internet transfers for the products on Google's data-portability list. (high confidence) (verified as of 2025-09-11) — https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/<object-id>/Appendix_N_-_Egress_fees___free_switching_programmes.pdf
- [statement] AWS and Google size the credit on the data stored when the request is made, so the credit covers moving each byte once. A migration that moves data more than once can exceed it, for example re-seeding, or a forward sync plus a reverse sync kept for rollback. That example is an inference from the CMA's reasoning. The CMA judged AWS and Google credits insufficient for temporary multi-cloud use during a switch. Microsoft told the CMA its program covers multi-cloud egress inside the 60-day window for a total switch. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-31) — https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/<object-id>/Appendix_N_-_Egress_fees___free_switching_programmes.pdf · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud, https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/free-data-transfer-out-to-internet-when-moving-out-of-aws/
- [statement] Respect the write rules or lose data. Atlas blocks writes on the destination when a live migration starts. Other clients must not write to the destination while mongosync runs. A write to the source during commit can cause data loss. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/api/commit/

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] The mongosync destination needs disk for the logical data plus the destination oplog entries the initial sync writes. The mongosync FAQ example: migrating 10 GB of data needs 10 GB for the data and another 10 GB for insert oplog entries. From mongosync 1.22, /start estimates on-disk size, applies a 1.25x safety factor, and returns InsufficientDestinationDiskSpace if the destination lacks room. skipDiskSpaceCheck: true turns the check off. The check is best effort only. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/
- [statement] MongoDB says the vast majority of Atlas customers spend less than 10% of their budget on data transfer (Atlas docs), and that data transfer fees are under 10% of the bill for most customers (AWS pricing page). These are vendor statements about steady-state spend, not about migrations. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/products/platform/atlas-cloud-providers/aws/pricing
- [statement] AWS gives credits for free data transfer out to the internet when a customer moves all of its data off AWS, or all of its data off one AWS service, across its eligible payer accounts. The customer asks AWS Support and does not have to close the account. AWS's page was updated on 10/8/26 to give non-EU customers 180 days to finish, and on 9/30/25 to drop the requirement of more than 100 GB/month of transfer. AWS says it applies additional scrutiny when the same account applies repeatedly. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-08) — https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/free-data-transfer-out-to-internet-when-moving-out-of-aws/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.fierce-network.com/data-center/aws-ditches-egress-fees-customers-who-leave, https://www.ciodive.com/news/microsoft-azure-eliminates-cloud-data-egress-fees/710367/
- [statement] Azure gives free internet egress to customers leaving Azure for another cloud or on-premises: the first 100 GB per month is free in all regions, and larger moves claim credits through Azure Support. When Microsoft announced the waiver in March 2024, press reports said the move had to finish within 60 days and that credits apply only after all Azure subscriptions on the account are cancelled. The current Azure pricing page does not repeat those two terms. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/bandwidth/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.ciodive.com/news/microsoft-azure-eliminates-cloud-data-egress-fees/710367/
- [statement] Estimate egress as gigabytes moved times the sending provider's per-GB rate. Arithmetic example, not a quoted figure: 10 TB (10,240 GB) out of Atlas on AWS at the $0.09-$0.16/GB internet list range is about $920-$1,640 before any waiver. mongosync's default network compression lowers wire bytes, and change-stream traffic during the overlap adds to them. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] MongoDB's worked example of a forced serverless-to-dedicated migration (50 GB, AWS us-east-1, help-center article dated 1 July 2025) bills a migration M50 cluster at $2.00/h for 24 h ($48.00), interim M40 and M30 clusters ($27.12 and $15.12), and data transfer at $0.01/GB (up to $5.00), total $95.24. It shows that Atlas bills a temporary oversized cluster by the hour and that auto-scaling through interim tiers adds line items. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-07-01) — https://intercom-help.mongodb.com/en/articles/11689655-serverless-to-dedicated-costs-explained
- [statement] mongosync protects small destinations: for migrations of 64 GB or less into destinations with 4 or fewer vCPUs, the collection copy issues fewer concurrent writes. Setting an explicit load level turns this off, and the user can change the load level during a sync. On Atlas destinations mongosync runs 12 createIndexes commands at once, capped by maxNumActiveUserIndexBuilds. Raising that value speeds index builds but raises destination CPU and can trigger unintended Atlas auto-scaling events. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/about-mongosync/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] The destination needs disk for the migrated data plus the insert oplog entries written during the initial sync. The docs example: a 10 GB migration needs at least 10 GB for data and another 10 GB for oplog entries. Budget roughly double the logical data size while the sync runs. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] Since mongosync 1.22, /start checks destination disk space. It estimates the on-disk size of the selected collections and indexes and applies a 1.25x safety factor. If space is short, /start returns InsufficientDestinationDiskSpace and the migration does not start. The skipDiskSpaceCheck option bypasses the check. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/
- [statement] For data sets under about 300 GB that can tolerate extended downtime, MongoDB recommends mongodump and mongorestore. It recommends mongoexport and mongoimport only when index handling is not a concern. These options trade cutover tooling for downtime. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] mongosync supports one-time migrations only. The destination cannot serve application reads or writes until commit succeeds and canWrite is true. MongoDB states that disaster recovery, analytics, and similar use cases are not supported workflows, so mongosync cannot keep a standing standby copy during a long dual-run. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/about-mongosync/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] Atlas Live Migration (pull) is the managed wrapper around mongosync: it needs little setup, the destination must be in Atlas, and the source may be on-premises or in Atlas. MongoDB recommends it for source clusters of 5 TB or less or up to 3 shards. It recommends standalone mongosync above those thresholds, and whenever the user must use VNet peering or Private Link, cannot allow a third party to reach the source, or will not import the source into Cloud Manager or Ops Manager. Standalone mongosync adds tunable parameters, pause and resume, detailed progress, direct logs, filtered sync, and a destination that may be on-premises, but the user hosts it. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/live-migration-comparison-modes/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration
- [statement] Pull live migration needs a publicly reachable source and cannot use VPC peering or private endpoints as the migration data path; both stay usable for application connectivity. The destination cannot be a Free or Flex cluster. Clusters on 'Latest Version With Auto Upgrades' are unsupported. MongoDB Search (Atlas Search) indexes are not migrated. Push live migration supports VPC peering or private endpoints between the migration host and Atlas, with private endpoints only within a single cloud provider and region. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/
- [statement] mongomirror reached end of life on 31 July 2025 and works only with MongoDB 6.0 and below; MongoDB says mongosync replaces it. mongomirror does not import users or roles, does not copy the config database, cannot move time-series data, and needs TTL indexes dropped and rebuilt. The Atlas architecture page still lists mongomirror as a manual migration tool without the end-of-life note. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/mongomirror/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration
- [statement] mongosync makes two round trips to the destination for each source operation, so latency between mongosync and the destination slows the sync. It uses majority reads and writes, so replica-set nodes spread across regions slow it further. It can run on hardware separate from either cluster, and it enables network compression by default when both clusters share a compressor. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] Size the source oplog window to cover the whole migration: raise the minimum oplog window when storage auto-scaling is on, or the fixed oplog size when it is off. If operations that mongosync has not applied roll off the source oplog, the sync fails. If a source outage or pause outlasts the oplog window, mongosync cannot resume, and the user must restart from the beginning, which removes all migrated data from the destination. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/
- [statement] The embedded verifier is on by default in mongosync (since 1.9) and keeps its state in memory. The limitations page sizes it at about 10 GB plus 500 MB per 1 million documents; the start-up disclaimer says about 0.5 GB per 1 million documents and that verification fails if memory is insufficient. Verification cannot resume after a pause or restart. Atlas Live Migration verifies by default and then needs a large destination oplog; the 'Verify data post-migration' switch turns it off. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/
- [statement] MongoDB's architecture page limits mongodump with mongorestore to data sets under about 300 GB that can tolerate extended downtime, and limits mongoexport with mongoimport to small data sets with no index concerns. These are the fallback paths when live migration cannot be used. (low confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration
- [statement] mongosync does not check that a deployment meets its limitations; running it in the presence of a limitation 'could lead to undefined behavior on the destination cluster', and the limits apply for the whole migration, including pauses. Operations that break or slow a sync include DDL on the source, movePrimary, moveChunk, moveRange, reshardCollection, shard-key refinement, rolling index builds, writes by other clients to the destination, and a balancer that is enabled after start. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] For parallel use of two providers, Art. 34(2) of the EU Data Act lets a provider charge data egress only to pass on egress costs incurred, without exceeding them. Recital 99 says egress for in-parallel use can be an ongoing activity, unlike the one-off egress of switching. Google points European customers to a separate Data Transfer Essentials offer for parallel use. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32023R2854 · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://cloud.google.com/exit-cloud
- [statement] mongosync does not sync users or roles, system.* collections, Atlas Search indexes, or Persistent Query Settings. It does not support time-series collections, clustered collections with expireAfterSeconds, Queryable Encryption, client-side field-level encryption, global clusters, or sync from a sharded cluster to a replica set. Each gap needs separate work after or instead of the sync, such as recreating users and roles and rebuilding search indexes on the destination. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/
- [statement] Vendor statements that egress is a minor part of switching cost are unmeasured for database migrations. Bloomberg reported Google's position that switching fees are about 2% of the total cost of migrating to a new provider. AWS said about 90% of its customers already pay nothing for data transfer out because of the 100 GB/month free allowance. Gartner's Lydia Leong said the cost of the move is trivial compared with the ongoing cost of storing data. None of these sources measured a database-cluster migration. (medium confidence) — https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/cloud/google-ends-cloud-switching-fees-pressuring-amazon-and-microsoft · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.fierce-network.com/data-center/aws-ditches-egress-fees-customers-who-leave, https://www.ciodive.com/news/microsoft-azure-eliminates-cloud-data-egress-fees/710367/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Atlas Live Migration carries no tool fee: the Atlas data-transfer docs call it 'the free Atlas Live Migration Service'. MongoDB's migration guidance frames the cost the user controls as destination-cluster sizing: temporary scaling during the sync, then resizing to the right tier after cutover. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration
- [statement] For the migration window, MongoDB recommends a destination Atlas tier at least two tiers above the source, at least an M40, and an M80 with 6000 IOPS disks or higher for large data sets. It tells users to disable auto-scaling on the destination during the migration and to set a large fixed oplog size or minimum oplog window there. Users may raise the destination tier temporarily and resize after cutover. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/architecture/current/migration
- [statement] While a live migration runs, Atlas pauses both scheduled and on-demand cloud backup snapshots of the target cluster. Atlas resumes them automatically after the cutover step. The destination takes no new Atlas snapshots during the overlap. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/
- [statement] mongosync copies unique indexes as non-unique indexes and restores uniqueness at commit. /progress returns canWrite: true once the indexes are set to prepareUnique, but the state reaches COMMITTED only after mongosync converts them to unique indexes. On large collections the conversion is resource intensive, so the gap between canWrite: true and COMMITTED can be long. Applications can write in the gap, but index builds wait and write latency can rise. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/cutover-process/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/mongosync-behavior/
- [statement] MongoDB suggests running the live-migration procedure twice. A first partial run stops before the cutover step and creates an up-to-date Atlas staging cluster for application tests. A second run performs the production cutover. The staging cluster is an extra Atlas cluster, so budget its run-rate for as long as it exists. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/
- [statement] Atlas docs list data transfer prices by provider (checked 2026-10-20). AWS clusters: same region $0.00-$0.01/GB, different region $0.02-$0.15/GB, out to internet $0.09-$0.16/GB. Azure clusters: internet data transfer $0.087-$0.181/GB. Google Cloud clusters: internet $0.12-$0.23/GB, between regions $0.02-$0.15/GB. The Atlas-on-AWS pricing page shows the base figures $0.01 same region, $0.02 cross-region, $0.09 internet. Ranges depend on region. Atlas charges no incoming transfer and charges no outgoing transfer on Free and Flex tiers. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/products/platform/atlas-cloud-providers/aws/pricing
- [statement] In a push live migration the user provisions, secures, and runs the migration host, and Cloud Manager must monitor the source cluster. MongoDB's push page requires source and destination at MongoDB 6.0.17 or later. AWS Prescriptive Guidance still says 6.0.8 or later for guided pull or push migration. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/import/c2c-push-live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/migration-mongodb-atlas/live-migration.html
- [statement] Budget a migration overlap from these documented terms: source run-rate, plus destination run-rate at least two tiers above the source, for the initial copy plus up to 120 hours of sync and the cutover window; destination disk for data plus sync oplog; a migration host for push or standalone mongosync; source-side egress; and a staging cluster if the user rehearses. MongoDB publishes no copy throughput and no downtime figure, so the duration term must come from a test run. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/faq/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/billing/data-transfer-costs/
- [statement] A migration started with reversible: true can be reversed after commit, which keeps the old cluster usable as a rollback target. Reversal needs the same number of shards and the same major version on both clusters and no filtered sync, and the user must not drop the mongosync metadata databases. The rollback window is therefore an extra dual-running period. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/about-mongosync/ · keywords: Migration and Cutover Cost (Live Migration, mongosync, Dual-Running, Egress) · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations/, https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/cutover-process/
